Smart in Public
In this episode of Smart in Public, the Katie's welcome Felicity Barber, the woman behind the speeches for leaders at Lloyd's of London, the Federal Reserve Banks of San Francisco and New York, and BlackRock. Today she runs Thoughtful Communications, where she writes speeches, coaches executives for the stage and trains corporate teams in public speaking.As comms people, we can all appreciate how in those rooms one wrong word can move a market, so we asked her how speechwriting works behind the scenes. Most of her answer was about trust. A CEO won't believe the words on the page until they believe the person who wrote them. So Felicity gets in the car with them, gets on the plane, sits in on meetings and keeps showing up until the relationship is there.Why this episode absolutely rips:🎯 One sentence at the top of every draft. Before the speech starts, Felicity writes the key message: what should the audience think at the end that they didn't think at the beginning?🏦 Storytelling in finance. Felicity often starts a finance speech with emotion, which makes plenty of people in financial services squirm. Her audiences include retail investors and entrepreneurs just dipping a toe in, and they need to understand what big institutions are doing on their behalf.🎤 The audience outside the room. The people who matter most may never sit in the audience. Felicity writes for university students while making sure regulators and financial journalists get the points they're looking for.🤝 Speeches become the narrative. A good speech often becomes how the company talks about an issue for months afterward. That's why Felicity brings in internal comms, investor relations, and the press team early.🤖 AI and the speechwriter. When one of her CEOs went through a crisis this year, they called Felicity and a PR partner they trusted -- not ChatGPT. Sure, AI can build her a business spreadsheet, but in her perspective is that it also made the writing harder, because now writers scrub out AI-sounding phrases on top of corporate jargon.🚶 What CEOs get wrong on stage. One is pacing in front of giant screens like it's a 2007 iPhone launch. Another is announcing great returns with a face like the dog just died.🙅 Words to retire. "Excited." "Thrive." Let's face it, most people are just trying to get through the day. And then there's "we're all like a family," which tends to come up shortly before the layoffs.💰 Money insight: Felicity wants speechwriters to talk openly about rates, especially women in the field, and to ask peers what they make, because pricing in this industry is hard to benchmark. Her red flags with a new client are haggling over every line item and a CEO who has already gone through five or six speechwriters. 1190: Fixing What Growth Tries to Hide | Jaylene Kunze, LegitScript
When Jaylene Kunze was asked to help rebuild a struggling subsidiary in the United Kingdom, she packed up her family and moved overseas with her nine-month-old daughter. The assignment was one more example of the type of challenge that would come to define her career. Rather than following a traditional finance path, Kunze gravitated toward what she calls “the fixer” role, stepping into situations where businesses needed operational repair, process improvement, or organizational change.
That mindset began to take shape through compliance and Sarbanes-Oxley work. While many viewed the documentation requirements as burdensome, Kunze tells us the process forced her to understand “the intersection of people, process, and systems” behind the numbers. It gave her visibility into how businesses actually operated and prepared her for increasingly complex leadership roles.
Read More
Her appetite for transformation became especially valuable when Tendril transitioned from venture-capital ownership to private-equity ownership. Kunze tells us the company ultimately combined six businesses into what became Uplight. As CFO, she oversaw diligence and integration while helping absorb five acquisitions within seven months.
The experience delivered lasting lessons. Culture, she tells us, matters more than many leaders expect. Different organizations often make decisions in entirely different ways, creating friction that financial models cannot predict. She also learned the cost of pushing too hard. Her team successfully completed aggressive integrations, but Kunze tells us she underestimated the human toll and would invest more heavily in staffing and support if given the opportunity again.
Today, those lessons continue to shape how she approaches leadership, growth, and change.

CFOTL: Tell us about LegitScript. What’s this company about?
Kunze: LegitScript is a really cool company. It’s mission-based, and our mission is to make the internet and the payments ecosystem safer. What does that mean? It means we’re looking for the bad actors—people who are selling, transacting, or producing illegal goods and services on the internet.
We focus primarily on high-risk areas such as online pharmacies, telemedicine, firearms, gambling, and adult-related businesses. We work with major platforms like Google, payment providers, banks, credit card companies, and individual businesses to identify bad actors and help remove them from the ecosystem, preventing them from processing payments or advertising online.
Read More
To make it more tangible, many people know someone who uses a med spa or takes a GLP-1 weight-loss medication. One of our business lines focuses on certifying those who sell medicine online and ensuring they are legitimate pharmacists, licensed physicians, or sourcing medications from certified pharmacies. Ultimately, it’s about protecting consumers and helping ensure they receive legitimate products and services.
CFOTL: Tell us a little about the company’s capital structure over time. Could you share some of that history?
Kunze: The company was founder-built and founder-owned. The founder eventually sold the business to private equity, and today we’re operating under our second private-equity ownership cycle.
CFOTL: If you had to boil it down, what’s driving growth inside the business today?
Kunze: There are a few drivers. First, AI is making it easier to be a bad actor. You can spin up a website and appear to be selling legitimate products in a matter of minutes. As a result, the need for organizations that can identify bad actors and help remove them from the ecosystem continues to grow.
Another major driver is the continued expansion of telemedicine and telehealth since COVID. A significant portion of healthcare interactions now occur virtually. That creates a need for stronger controls and certification processes to ensure providers are legitimate and consumers are receiving real healthcare services and authentic medications.
CFOTL: We always like to ask about metrics. What are the input metrics you watch most closely?
Kunze: There are several. As a SaaS business, we monitor the standard metrics such as gross retention, net retention, and overall growth. What’s particularly important for us is that we operate three distinct product lines, so I spend a great deal of time evaluating product-line performance.
Product-line reporting is much harder than many people realize. This is probably the fifth company where I’ve worked to build reporting that goes beyond contribution margin and all the way down to understanding what each product line contributes to the bottom line. Each of our product lines is at a different stage of its lifecycle. One is growing very quickly, one is relatively stable, and another is dealing with pricing pressure.
That creates important resource-allocation decisions. We don’t want to starve a fast-growing product line in order to support another area unnecessarily. A significant part of my focus is understanding those tradeoffs, evaluating performance at the product-line level, and making sure we’re investing resources where they’ll create the greatest long-term value.

1190: Fixing What Growth Tries to Hide |  Jaylene Kunze, LegitScript
1190: Fixing What Growth Tries to Hide | Jaylene Kunze, LegitScript
When Jaylene Kunze was asked to help rebuild a struggling subsidiary in the United Kingdom, she packed up her family and moved overseas with her nine-month-old daughter. The assignment was one more example of the type of challenge that would come to define her career. Rather than following a traditional finance path, Kunze gravitated toward what she calls “the fixer” role, stepping into situations where businesses needed operational repair, process improvement, or organizational change.
That mindset began to take shape through compliance and Sarbanes-Oxley work. While many viewed the documentation requirements as burdensome, Kunze tells us the process forced her to understand “the intersection of people, process, and systems” behind the numbers. It gave her visibility into how businesses actually operated and prepared her for increasingly complex leadership roles.
Read More
Her appetite for transformation became especially valuable when Tendril transitioned from venture-capital ownership to private-equity ownership. Kunze tells us the company ultimately combined six businesses into what became Uplight. As CFO, she oversaw diligence and integration while helping absorb five acquisitions within seven months.
The experience delivered lasting lessons. Culture, she tells us, matters more than many leaders expect. Different organizations often make decisions in entirely different ways, creating friction that financial models cannot predict. She also learned the cost of pushing too hard. Her team successfully completed aggressive integrations, but Kunze tells us she underestimated the human toll and would invest more heavily in staffing and support if given the opportunity again.
Today, those lessons continue to shape how she approaches leadership, growth, and change.

CFOTL: Tell us about LegitScript. What’s this company about?
Kunze: LegitScript is a really cool company. It’s mission-based, and our mission is to make the internet and the payments ecosystem safer. What does that mean? It means we’re looking for the bad actors—people who are selling, transacting, or producing illegal goods and services on the internet.
We focus primarily on high-risk areas such as online pharmacies, telemedicine, firearms, gambling, and adult-related businesses. We work with major platforms like Google, payment providers, banks, credit card companies, and individual businesses to identify bad actors and help remove them from the ecosystem, preventing them from processing payments or advertising online.
Read More
To make it more tangible, many people know someone who uses a med spa or takes a GLP-1 weight-loss medication. One of our business lines focuses on certifying those who sell medicine online and ensuring they are legitimate pharmacists, licensed physicians, or sourcing medications from certified pharmacies. Ultimately, it’s about protecting consumers and helping ensure they receive legitimate products and services.
CFOTL: Tell us a little about the company’s capital structure over time. Could you share some of that history?
Kunze: The company was founder-built and founder-owned. The founder eventually sold the business to private equity, and today we’re operating under our second private-equity ownership cycle.
CFOTL: If you had to boil it down, what’s driving growth inside the business today?
Kunze: There are a few drivers. First, AI is making it easier to be a bad actor. You can spin up a website and appear to be selling legitimate products in a matter of minutes. As a result, the need for organizations that can identify bad actors and help remove them from the ecosystem continues to grow.
Another major driver is the continued expansion of telemedicine and telehealth since COVID. A significant portion of healthcare interactions now occur virtually. That creates a need for stronger controls and certification processes to ensure providers are legitimate and consumers are receiving real healthcare services and authentic medications.
CFOTL: We always like to ask about metrics. What are the input metrics you watch most closely?
Kunze: There are several. As a SaaS business, we monitor the standard metrics such as gross retention, net retention, and overall growth. What’s particularly important for us is that we operate three distinct product lines, so I spend a great deal of time evaluating product-line performance.
Product-line reporting is much harder than many people realize. This is probably the fifth company where I’ve worked to build reporting that goes beyond contribution margin and all the way down to understanding what each product line contributes to the bottom line. Each of our product lines is at a different stage of its lifecycle. One is growing very quickly, one is relatively stable, and another is dealing with pricing pressure.
That creates important resource-allocation decisions. We don’t want to starve a fast-growing product line in order to support another area unnecessarily. A significant part of my focus is understanding those tradeoffs, evaluating performance at the product-line level, and making sure we’re investing resources where they’ll create the greatest long-term value.

COFO Era: Why a Risky, Rewarding Dual Role Is Taking Over the C-Suite
July 24, 2026
Author: Anthony Noto | Photos: Global Finance Media
Image 5: TwitterImage 6: FacebookImage 7: LinkedInImage 8: Email
Finance leaders are taking over operations—and the new COFO role isn't a simple shortcut.
There’s a new acronym roaming the C-suite. The so-called COFO — a hybrid chief operating and financial officer — is more common than ever, marking a structural shift in how companies are deciding who runs the business. But the combined role is a risky one: it works far better going one direction than the other, industry watchers tell _Global Finance_.
Salesforce made it official last year. The San Francisco-based company named Robin Washington its first COFO — tasking a 30-year finance veteran with steering both the balance sheet and the company’s artificial intelligence (AI) and digital-labor transformation.
PayPal, headquartered in San Jose, California, took a similar route. The company expanded CFO Jamie Miller’s mandate to cover operations as well as finance, putting one executive in charge of the strategic growth initiatives that used to require two separate memos and a joint meeting to sort out. Two very different companies, same conclusion: the boss who understands the cash is likely the person who’s expected to move it.
While some observers view this trend as temporary, many industry leaders see the hybrid COFO as a permanent shift in corporate leadership.
“I do think this is a trend that’s here to stay,” said Jaylene Kunze, COFO at Portland, Oregon-based LegitScript, a risk management service.
For decades, the CFO and COO occupied a kind of awkward office marriage: sharing a roof, splitting the chores, occasionally blaming each other when the numbers didn’t add up.
“Historically, the CFO and COO were often set up to work against each other by default since each one’s success depended on the other, but neither had the full picture needed to make the best decisions for the company,” Kunze added.
That being said: Does the COO job disappear? Kunze calls “operational acumen and a real connection” to the business as “essential.” However, she argues the CFO seat has evolved past spreadsheets and GAAP.
“That’s exactly why the COFO role is emerging as such a powerful one,” she said. “It’s not enough to build the model; you must know what growth targets you’re driving toward and which levers to pull, when, and how.”
‘A Whole New Job’
Executive coach Edith Hamilton, who works with CFOs and COOs at NEXT New Growth, noticed the same pattern.
“It’s not title inflation. It’s authority redistribution,” she said, pointing to AI-driven process change as a major accelerant. But the honeymoon, she warns, is short.
“The second emotion is, ‘Oh dear Lord, this is a whole new job.'” Boards, she added, flip the script overnight — from “protect the numbers” to “use your authority to change the business.”
Her verdict: durable, but not universal. “It will work in companies where finance and operations need to be welded together — not merely coordinated.”
Sierra Hinson has been living this arrangement for over a decade under various titles. Most recently, as a “fractional CFOO” through her firm, Additive Insights. Her reaction to the sudden buzz? “What took so long?” Splitting finance and operations creates blind spots and slows everyone down, she said. And it shows up at the worst possible moment — the exit. “In a transaction, buyers look for inconsistency between what the financials say and what the operations show,” she said. “The title is the easy part — the track record is not.”
Missing the Point
Not everyone’s convinced the direction of travel could reverse. Ariela Tannenbaum, former CFO at Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati and now a profitability architect, thinks the whole debate is arguing about the wrong things. “The COFO debate misses the point on two counts,” she said. “First, titles. Whether you call it inflation or evolution, a title reflects accountability, not capability. The higher the title, the greater the responsibility. Rebranding a role does not dilute it; it expands it.”
Her second point takes aim at the assumption that AI is what’s really behind all this. “Faster information is not faster judgment,” Tannenbaum said. “A CFO or COO in a COFO role will spend exactly as much time reviewing, analyzing, validating, and deciding as before. AI compresses the data cycle. The thinking, judgment, and responsibility cycle remains unchanged.”
What’s actually driving the trend, she argues, is something more old-fashioned: good managers building good benches. “Great financial leaders already mentor, elevate, and develop their teams to the point where the CFO can spread his or her wings to take on an expanded operational mandate,” she said. Given the chance herself, she wouldn’t blink: “I would run the operation with conviction through the financial lens, where clarity lives.”
The Risk of Reversing the COFO Role
But Tannenbaum, like Hamilton, sees the arrangement working in only one direction. “Can an experienced CFO absorb the COO role? Absolutely,” she said. “Capital discipline, resource allocation, performance accountability — these are financial constructs applied operationally.”
The reverse, however, is not symmetrical.
A COO assuming the COFO role introduces real risk: technical gaps in financial analysis, regulatory exposure, and the kind of judgment calls that only come from deep financial experience.
Her bottom line: “The COFO is not a shortcut. But it works in one direction far better than the other.” And for companies simply focused on saving a salary line rather than building real bench strength, she has a warning dressed up as a punchline: “Can’t find two great executives? Look under the light.”
Which brings the debate back to a question. Firms like Ridgeway Financial Service ask CEOs: does your team just report the numbers, or help run the business? Increasingly, in this new hybrid role, the answer is both — same office, same person, one very full inbox.

1226: Anaplan's Growth Equation: AI, Profitability, and Scale | Hemant Kapadia, CFO, Anaplan
For Anaplan CFO Hemant Kapadia, one of the more revealing measures of the company’s transformation isn’t revenue growth alone. It’s the fact that Anaplan has nearly the same number of employees it had when it was taken private in 2022—even as annual recurring revenue has grown from approximately $600 million toward $1.4 billion. The company has also become materially more profitable, generating free cash flow margins in the mid-30s. That financial flexibility has helped fund a $500 million investment commitment spanning infrastructure, platform development, new applications, and artificial intelligence. Yet Kapadia’s ambitions extend beyond Anaplan’s product roadmap. Drawing on an engineering background and 14 years at General Electric, he has long viewed financial performance through an operational lens. Today, that perspective informs Anaplan’s internal AI Readiness program, an initiative he leads to identify opportunities for redesigning processes across the business. Rather than treating AI as another cost-reduction exercise, Kapadia wants employees to reconsider how work gets done—and which activities deserve their attention. “Our approach is not to say we’re gonna implement AI and we’re gonna cut, you know, thirty percent of the organization,” he explains. There’s a similar philosophy behind Anaplan’s own financial operations. By connecting sales forecasts, customer bookings, workforce costs, and cloud expenses, Kapadia says he effectively has a daily financial close, allowing investment decisions to be made during a quarter rather than after it ends. Looking ahead, his challenge is whether Anaplan can double or triple its business while keeping employee growth far below historical norms. For Kapadia, AI’s promise isn’t simply doing the same work faster. It’s changing what the organization can accomplish.

Evan Goldberg on the End of ERP as We Know It
At SuiteWorld 2026, NetSuite’s founder outlines how AI is transforming business software—and what the shift means for CFOs. When Evan Goldberg, founder and executive vice president of Oracle NetSuite, declares that ERP as we know it is over, the statement carries particular weight. Goldberg helped pioneer cloud-based enterprise software in 1998, challenging the conventional wisdom about how businesses should manage their financial and operational systems. Nearly three decades later, he sees artificial intelligence driving an equally consequential transformation. Speaking with CFO Thought Leader at SuiteWorld 2026 in Las Vegas, Goldberg described a future in which ERP systems do more than organize information, automate transactions, and generate reports. Increasingly, they will anticipate problems, recommend solutions, and execute work—with human oversight. Read More To Goldberg, the transformation rests on three developments: AI becoming the primary user interface, ERP becoming tailored to individual businesses, and software gaining the ability to perform more work autonomously. The implications extend well beyond technology. Goldberg believes finance teams will increasingly apply their analytical capabilities across the enterprise, identifying operational issues before they affect financial results. He also sees the traditional month-end close giving way to more continuous financial visibility. Rather than focusing exclusively on achieving a zero-day close, Goldberg argues that CFOs should consider how accurately their systems can reflect the business throughout the reporting period. That shift could fundamentally change how finance contributes to decision-making. “We’re really trying to free up the CFO from firefighting mode to strategic analysis mode,” Goldberg explained. For CFOs, the emerging opportunity is not simply to automate existing responsibilities. It is to redirect financial expertise toward decisions that shape business performance—while increasingly intelligent systems handle more of the underlying work.

1225: Nix the Clicks: Building a Finance Function That Manages by Exception | Steve Fox, CFO, Every Man Jack
When Steve Fox joined Every Man Jack in 2021, the men’s personal care brand had a new private equity owner and an ambitious growth agenda. Carlyle Group saw an opportunity: a widely distributed brand that had never invested heavily in marketing. The challenge was finding the operating leverage to fund that investment. For Fox, the answer increasingly lies in technology. At Every Man Jack, a company known for its outdoor-inspired grooming products, the finance team has remained at five employees even as transaction volume has tripled. Fox credits investments in technology and a growing emphasis on automation. The initiative even has a name: “Nix the Clicks by 26.” The goal is to eliminate manual transactions and replace traditional workflows with functional command centers where employees supervise automated processes, investigate exceptions, and monitor business performance. The transformation gathered momentum after Every Man Jack implemented NetSuite in September 2025. A month later, at SuiteWorld, the company’s IT manager connected the new ERP platform to emerging AI capabilities. Still, Fox recognizes that easier access to technology brings its own complications. With roughly 70 employees suddenly capable of creating software-driven solutions, the company established an AI oversight committee to prevent duplication and keep experimentation aligned with strategy. It’s a distinctly operational approach from a CFO whose career began in public accounting before taking him into retail management and high-growth businesses. And while Fox is enthusiastic about what technology makes possible, his guiding principle remains decidedly human: successful adoption begins with investing in people.

1224: Building a Cybersecurity Leader for the AI Era | Joe Iantosca, CFO, Cyera
When Joe Iantosca arrived at Cyera as CFO, his first hire wasn't an accountant or an FP&A professional. It was a data engineer. For Iantosca, the decision reflected a conviction formed over years of working inside technology companies: Finance cannot help steer a business without reliable access to the information driving it. That conviction first took shape at Palantir, where he witnessed the impact of centralizing financial and operational data. At BetterCloud, where his responsibilities eventually expanded into the COO role, he carried the lesson further, connecting product, marketing, and business information into a common analytical foundation. At Cyera, that experience has become especially relevant. The five-year-old cybersecurity company operates across 15 countries, employs approximately 2,000 people, and has completed seven acquisitions. Its ambition is to build a comprehensive AI security platform that helps enterprises adopt artificial intelligence while protecting sensitive data. For Iantosca, financing that expansion involves more than allocating capital. It means understanding how customers are acquired, how products reach the market, and how new offerings become commercially successful. His operating background has also made him unusually comfortable entering customer conversations and examining the friction that can slow enterprise sales. Meanwhile, the company's investment in centralized data is helping finance pursue AI-driven automation, including potentially significant changes to the month-end close. The challenge ahead is balancing experimentation with financial discipline. Cyera encourages employees to test new ideas and move quickly, but major investments require evidence. Iantosca's priorities reflect that balance: adaptability, discipline, and the successful commercialization of new products.

1223: Scaling Sokin: Beyond the First $100 Million | Tom Steer, CFO, Sokin
When Tom Steer joined Sokin as CFO, he already knew the international payments company unusually well. As an investment banker at FT Partners, he had advised Sokin through a capital raise during a difficult period for fintech funding. He knew its leadership, its financial projections, and the ambitions behind its growth. What he had yet to experience was the challenge of building a finance organization capable of keeping pace. Sokin helps multinational businesses manage cross-border payments, currencies, and treasury operations across fragmented banking systems. Its infrastructure supports payments to 170 countries, while a growing embedded-finance offering allows other companies to bring Sokin’s capabilities to their own customers. For Steer, the challenge is deciding where to place the next investment. North America has emerged as Sokin’s fastest-growing market, while embedded payments and AI-enabled treasury tools present additional opportunities. Each requires capital, talent, and organizational attention. The assumptions behind those decisions can change quickly. An anticipated shortage of engineers, for example, became less pressing as AI improved productivity, shifting attention toward sales and partnerships. Inside finance, Steer encountered a different constraint: a lean team trying to accomplish too much. Three months into the role, he and his finance director stepped away from their daily responsibilities to map the work ahead. “We can’t get this done on our own,” he recalls. Today, Steer is building systems and teams designed for substantially greater transaction volumes. His guiding question is less about what finance can accomplish today than whether its infrastructure will still work when the business doubles in size.

1222: Scaling Through Acquisitions, Integration, and AI | Kara Childress, CFO, Vensure Employment Solutions
At Vensure Employer Solutions, completing an acquisition is only the beginning. The company has acquired roughly 120 businesses in eight years, and each new addition enters an integration process containing some 1,400 steps. For CFO and President Kara Childress, the challenge is not simply bringing more companies into the fold. It is making certain the organization can absorb them without multiplying its own inefficiencies. That challenge has become familiar territory for Childress, whose career took an unusual turn when she left public accounting to join Vensure as COO. Having previously served as the company’s outside auditor, she knew its finances. Operations offered something different: an opportunity to remove roadblocks and help people perform better. As Vensure expanded into global payroll, HR technology, and human capital management services, Childress’s responsibilities broadened to include finance and the presidency. Along the way, she confronted a finance organization whose regional and divisional structure was duplicating work. The acquisition engine was not slowing down. The finance organization needed to change before further growth made its existing structure untenable. “We need to think about this differently,” Childress recalls. The resulting reorganization reduced duplication and positioned finance to support additional acquisitions without continually adding staff. Meanwhile, a dedicated integration accounting team now brings acquired businesses into a common reporting framework beginning in their first month. Today, Vensure is also expanding its AI capabilities while Childress concentrates on client retention, organic growth, and sales investment. For a company accustomed to acquiring businesses, the next test is making its growing organization work better.
1222: Scaling Through Acquisitions, Integration, and AI | Kara Childress, CFO, Vensure Employment Solutions
7. Oct 14
1221: Rebuilding Bread Financial’s Capital Foundation—And What It Made Possible | Perry Beberman, CFO, Bread Financial
When Perry Beberman arrived at what is now Bread Financial, the company had a balance sheet problem. It was carrying too much leverage, had insufficient capital, and needed a more disciplined approach to funding its lending business. For a finance executive who had spent decades navigating consumer credit cycles, the assignment was familiar territory. The scale of the transformation, however, would demand patience. Today, Beberman points to a substantially different financial foundation. Bread has paid down more than 70% of its parent-company debt, built capital beyond established targets, and shifted direct-to-consumer deposits from less than 5% of funding in 2020 to more than half. The changes have given Bread greater capacity to invest in technology, support growth, and return capital to shareholders. Still, Beberman is quick to explain that financial discipline is not simply about strengthening a balance sheet. At Bread, whose products include co-branded credit cards, private-label cards, and installment lending, the daily challenge is balancing the ambitions of retail partners with the economics of consumer credit. Retailers want more approvals. Credit executives must manage losses. Finance must determine where the returns justify the risk. “They collide all the time,” Beberman says of those competing priorities. For him, such disagreements are not organizational failures. They are essential to making better decisions. That philosophy also shapes Bread’s adoption of AI, its continuing finance transformation, and its approach to capital allocation. Technology may accelerate analysis and automate routine work, but Beberman sees little reason to surrender judgment. After nearly four decades in finance, his operating principle remains remarkably consistent: growth matters, but only when the economics support it.
1221: Rebuilding Bread Financial’s Capital Foundation—And What It Made Possible | Perry Beberman, CFO, Bread Financial

1220: At Hippo, Growth and Risk Work Together | Guy Zeltser, CFO, Hippo Insurance
In 2023, Hippo faced what CFO Guy Zeltser describes as perhaps the worst quarter in the insurance company’s history. The response was not to chase growth harder. Instead, leadership made a decision that would have seemed counterintuitive during the company’s earlier expansion: shrink part of the business. Between 2023 and 2024, homeowners insurance premiums declined approximately 30% as Hippo recalibrated the risks it was willing to carry. For Zeltser, the decision marked a turning point in a broader transformation—one that would move the company toward profitability and a more diversified business model. Today, Hippo supports more than 60 insurance programs, generating fees and commissions alongside underwriting and investment income. That mix matters. Fee revenue offers greater predictability, while improved underwriting performance gives the company confidence to retain additional insurance risk. Zeltser’s approach reflects an unusual career path. Before McKinsey and corporate finance, he worked in his family’s toy business, where customer complaints and everyday transactions made the consequences of business decisions tangible. At McKinsey, another lesson emerged: even a board-approved strategy could stall when short-term financial targets overwhelmed longer-term investment. Both experiences inform his current agenda. Hippo is also deploying AI across claims and finance operations. Zeltser reports that AI now handles more than 80% of initial loss notifications, while finance has shortened its quarterly reporting timeline. With Hippo targeting a threefold or fourfold increase in profitability between 2026 and 2028, Zeltser faces a familiar tension: delivering quarterly results without sacrificing the investments required to build a larger business.

1190: Fixing What Growth Tries to Hide |  Jaylene Kunze, LegitScript
1190: Fixing What Growth Tries to Hide | Jaylene Kunze, LegitScript
When Jaylene Kunze was asked to help rebuild a struggling subsidiary in the United Kingdom, she packed up her family and moved overseas with her nine-month-old daughter. The assignment was one more example of the type of challenge that would come to define her career. Rather than following a traditional finance path, Kunze gravitated toward what she calls “the fixer” role, stepping into situations where businesses needed operational repair, process improvement, or organizational change.
That mindset began to take shape through compliance and Sarbanes-Oxley work. While many viewed the documentation requirements as burdensome, Kunze tells us the process forced her to understand “the intersection of people, process, and systems” behind the numbers. It gave her visibility into how businesses actually operated and prepared her for increasingly complex leadership roles.
Read More
Her appetite for transformation became especially valuable when Tendril transitioned from venture-capital ownership to private-equity ownership. Kunze tells us the company ultimately combined six businesses into what became Uplight. As CFO, she oversaw diligence and integration while helping absorb five acquisitions within seven months.
The experience delivered lasting lessons. Culture, she tells us, matters more than many leaders expect. Different organizations often make decisions in entirely different ways, creating friction that financial models cannot predict. She also learned the cost of pushing too hard. Her team successfully completed aggressive integrations, but Kunze tells us she underestimated the human toll and would invest more heavily in staffing and support if given the opportunity again.
Today, those lessons continue to shape how she approaches leadership, growth, and change.

CFOTL: Tell us about LegitScript. What’s this company about?
Kunze: LegitScript is a really cool company. It’s mission-based, and our mission is to make the internet and the payments ecosystem safer. What does that mean? It means we’re looking for the bad actors—people who are selling, transacting, or producing illegal goods and services on the internet.
We focus primarily on high-risk areas such as online pharmacies, telemedicine, firearms, gambling, and adult-related businesses. We work with major platforms like Google, payment providers, banks, credit card companies, and individual businesses to identify bad actors and help remove them from the ecosystem, preventing them from processing payments or advertising online.
Read More
To make it more tangible, many people know someone who uses a med spa or takes a GLP-1 weight-loss medication. One of our business lines focuses on certifying those who sell medicine online and ensuring they are legitimate pharmacists, licensed physicians, or sourcing medications from certified pharmacies. Ultimately, it’s about protecting consumers and helping ensure they receive legitimate products and services.
CFOTL: Tell us a little about the company’s capital structure over time. Could you share some of that history?
Kunze: The company was founder-built and founder-owned. The founder eventually sold the business to private equity, and today we’re operating under our second private-equity ownership cycle.
CFOTL: If you had to boil it down, what’s driving growth inside the business today?
Kunze: There are a few drivers. First, AI is making it easier to be a bad actor. You can spin up a website and appear to be selling legitimate products in a matter of minutes. As a result, the need for organizations that can identify bad actors and help remove them from the ecosystem continues to grow.
Another major driver is the continued expansion of telemedicine and telehealth since COVID. A significant portion of healthcare interactions now occur virtually. That creates a need for stronger controls and certification processes to ensure providers are legitimate and consumers are receiving real healthcare services and authentic medications.
CFOTL: We always like to ask about metrics. What are the input metrics you watch most closely?
Kunze: There are several. As a SaaS business, we monitor the standard metrics such as gross retention, net retention, and overall growth. What’s particularly important for us is that we operate three distinct product lines, so I spend a great deal of time evaluating product-line performance.
Product-line reporting is much harder than many people realize. This is probably the fifth company where I’ve worked to build reporting that goes beyond contribution margin and all the way down to understanding what each product line contributes to the bottom line. Each of our product lines is at a different stage of its lifecycle. One is growing very quickly, one is relatively stable, and another is dealing with pricing pressure.
That creates important resource-allocation decisions. We don’t want to starve a fast-growing product line in order to support another area unnecessarily. A significant part of my focus is understanding those tradeoffs, evaluating performance at the product-line level, and making sure we’re investing resources where they’ll create the greatest long-term value.

NEW YORK, Nov. 1, 2022 /PRNewswire/ -- Urbint, the leading AI platform for predicting and stopping threats to critical infrastructure and workers, has hired Jaylene Kunze as Chief Financial Officer. Kunze was previously CFO at Uplight, which provides software solutions to 80+ electric and gas utilities, and sold for $1.5 billion in 2021. I'm very excited about where Urbint is today, and where we're going to go."
Kunze led Tendril's growth as CFO for three years, and spearheaded its merger with Simple Energy to form Uplight. Prior to that, Kunze held financial leadership roles at engineering firm MWH Global, and other companies.

Google will recognise LegitScript Healthcare Certification for telemedicine providers in Spain from Aug. 5, 2026, LegitScript said today, opening paid search and display inventory to a category that had no compliant route onto the platform in the country. The change makes Spain the eleventh market where the certification functions as a gate on healthcare advertising.
The certification firm, headquartered in Portland, Oregon, described the arrangement as an expanded partnership with Google covering telemedicine businesses operating in the Spanish jurisdiction. Under the update, those businesses may apply for LegitScript Healthcare Certification and then promote their services across Google advertising platforms.
Eligibility to apply for LegitScript certification was never the constraint. Providers in Spain could already seek the credential. What changes on Aug. 5 is the platform side: according to LegitScript, Google's policy update marks the first time the certification will be recognised as part of Google's advertising approval process for providers in Spain.
That distinction matters commercially. A certification that no platform accepts produces no advertising access. The value of the credential in a given market is set almost entirely by whether the dominant search platform treats it as sufficient evidence of compliance.
What the certification requires
LegitScript's Healthcare Certification runs as a documented review rather than a self-attestation. According to the company, the process involves submitting an application, providing documentation to verify licensure and business legitimacy, and demonstrating adherence to patient privacy, clinical practices, and marketing integrity standards.
Those four review categories are the operative constraint for any Spanish provider weighing whether to pursue the credential. Licensure verification is the most objective of them. Patient privacy and clinical practice standards involve assessment against criteria that sit outside the advertising relationship altogether, which is precisely why platforms outsource the work.
Jaylene Kunze, Chief Operating and Financial Officer at LegitScript, framed the expansion in terms of the company's existing global footprint. "Through our partnership with Google, we're giving telemedicine providers around the world a safer path to online advertising," Kunze said. "Bringing our certification program to Spain advances our mission to help providers demonstrate compliance, advertise responsibly, and build trust with patients."
Angela Salter, Vice President of Enterprise Certification Sales and Partnerships at the company, addressed the demand side. "As global demand for telemedicine services ramps up, providers need safe avenues to reach patients online and advertise responsibly," Salter said. "Backed by our technology, proprietary data, and human expertise, LegitScript Certification allows providers to build credibility, connect with more patients through Google's ad platform, and navigate rapidly evolving healthcare regulations."
The market figure and its source
LegitScript cited a projected compound annual growth rate of 11.6% for the Spanish telehealth sector from 2026 to 2033, characterising Spain as an emerging key digital health market in Europe.
The figure carries a caveat worth stating plainly. It appears in a certification vendor's announcement of a product expansion into that same market, and the underlying research source is not identified in the press release. Growth projections extending seven years into a healthcare services category depend heavily on regulatory assumptions that no forecaster controls. Readers evaluating the Spanish opportunity should treat the number as the sponsor's framing rather than an independent measurement.
What the figure does establish is why Spain arrived on the list when it did. Certification programmes expand where the addressable base of paying applicants justifies the operational cost of building market-specific review criteria.
An eleventh market on a lengthening list
The press release positions the Spain move as following recent expansions in India and New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and Indonesia and the Philippines. LegitScript said certification is already required for telemedicine providers and online pharmacies using Google Ads in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, France, Australia, New Zealand, Indonesia, the Philippines, India and South Africa.
Spain becomes the eleventh entry on that list.
The sequence is legible from prior coverage. Google permitted LegitScript-certified telemedicine providers to promote services in France from Oct. 10, 2023, in what was then a narrow European opening. Australian online pharmacies and telemedicine providers came under the same certification requirement in 2024, with a 90-day grace period for existing advertisers and a seven-day warning before any suspension.
Japan added a dual pathway from January 2025, under which online pharmacies could qualify either through a valid pharmacy licence with active Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare registration or through LegitScript certification. Canada's addiction treatment category was brought into the framework in February 2025, with LegitScript operating as the verification partner across Google, Meta and Microsoft.
The United Kingdom and Singapore followed in July 2025, after a June 25 announcement. Under that update, UK telemedicine services moved to an "Allowed with limitations" classification, with the policy stating that Google permits promotion of prescription drug services by providers certified through LegitScript's Healthcare Merchant Certification Program while barring promotion of prescription drugs in ads and landing pages.
Most recently, Google opened advertising to pharmacies in India and telemedicine providers in New Zealand in an April 8, 2026 announcement, with the platform policy update expected that same month. That coverage noted LegitScript reported a 103% increase in certified healthcare organisations over the preceding year, and that the firm holds recognition from Visa and Mastercard for card-not-present transaction assessment.
Why platforms outsource the review
The pattern across these markets is consistent, and it is not primarily about healthcare. It is about where liability for compliance assessment sits.
Google's healthcare advertising rules require the platform to distinguish a licensed telemedicine operation from an unlicensed one across dozens of jurisdictions with distinct licensing registries, prescribing rules and privacy statutes. Building that capability in-house for every market is a substantial fixed cost with no advertising revenue attached to it. Delegating the determination to a specialist creates a single interface the platform can apply uniformly.
The consequence for advertisers is a two-stage approval sequence. Certification first, platform certification second. In the India and New Zealand expansion, LegitScript-certified organisations became eligible to apply for Google certification once the platform policy updated - the credential functions as a prerequisite, not as approval in itself.
Google has been recalibrating the surrounding rules throughout the period. The platform launched restricted drug term certification for personalised pharmaceutical targeting in the United States, Canada and New Zealand in July 2025, applying it across Google Ads and Display & Video 360. It then deprecated the Restricted Medical Content label in August 2025, stating the change was intended to simplify internal enforcement for keyword-targeting enablement while preserving existing certification requirements.
In October 2025, Google revised prescription drug advertising rules for Canada, New Zealand and the United States, permitting promotional use of prescription drug terms in those three markets. Programmatic buyers received parallel treatment in January 2026, when an Authorized Buyers policy change removed the third-party verification layer for certain pharmaceutical categories.
The direction is not uniform loosening. Certification requirements expand in some categories while approval friction falls in others, and the two movements are largely independent.
Spain's existing position in Google's healthcare rules
Spain was not absent from Google's healthcare advertising framework before this update. The country gained permission for melatonin dietary supplement advertising alongside Germany and France in an October 2025 change, effective November 2025. That coverage noted Spain does not require pharmacy certification for dietary supplement advertising while maintaining restrictions on other product categories.
Spain also appeared among the nine markets eligible for personal lubricant advertising under the sexual health policy expansion announced Oct. 28, 2024 and effective Nov. 11, 2024. Prescription medications for erectile dysfunction and hypoactive sexual desire disorder under that same policy were confined to Canada, New Zealand and the United States.
The telemedicine gap was therefore specific rather than general. Spanish advertisers could reach consumers with certain regulated health products but had no recognised compliance route for promoting virtual consultation services.
What the announcement does not address
Several operational questions remain unresolved in the source material.
The press release does not specify a grace period for Spanish advertisers already running telemedicine campaigns, nor does it state whether the seven-day suspension warning applied in Australia and other markets extends to Spain. It does not disclose certification pricing, application processing times, or the volume of Spanish providers expected to qualify.
Nor does the announcement address prescription drug promotion. In the United Kingdom, Singapore, India and New Zealand implementations, direct promotion of prescription drugs in ad copy and landing pages remained prohibited even for certified providers. Whether Spain follows the same restriction is not stated in the materials LegitScript issued, and providers will need Google's published country-specific guidance to determine it.
What this means for the marketing community
For agencies handling Spanish healthcare accounts, the practical effect is a new billable compliance workstream with a fixed date attached. Certification cannot be completed retroactively, and campaigns cannot launch before the credential clears.
For the broader search market, the update extends a structural shift that has been building since 2023. Access to advertising inventory in regulated verticals increasingly depends on third-party credentials rather than platform review alone. The bottleneck moves from the ad account to the certifying organisation, and campaign timelines become dependent on an approval process the advertiser cannot escalate through platform support.
That dependency concentrates influence. A single private certifier now stands between telemedicine providers and Google's advertising inventory across eleven markets, with recognition from Visa, Mastercard, social platforms and marketplaces layered on top. No published data establishes how long Spanish applications will take to process or what proportion will be approved, which leaves the practical width of the new channel unknown until the first cohort clears review.
Spain's telehealth operators will find out from Aug. 5.

1190: Fixing What Growth Tries to Hide | Jaylene Kunze, LegitScript
When Jaylene Kunze was asked to help rebuild a struggling subsidiary in the United Kingdom, she packed up her family and moved overseas with her nine-month-old daughter. The assignment was one more example of the type of challenge that would come to define her career. Rather than following a traditional finance path, Kunze gravitated toward what she calls “the fixer” role, stepping into situations where businesses needed operational repair, process improvement, or organizational change.
That mindset began to take shape through compliance and Sarbanes-Oxley work. While many viewed the documentation requirements as burdensome, Kunze tells us the process forced her to understand “the intersection of people, process, and systems” behind the numbers. It gave her visibility into how businesses actually operated and prepared her for increasingly complex leadership roles.
Read More
Her appetite for transformation became especially valuable when Tendril transitioned from venture-capital ownership to private-equity ownership. Kunze tells us the company ultimately combined six businesses into what became Uplight. As CFO, she oversaw diligence and integration while helping absorb five acquisitions within seven months.
The experience delivered lasting lessons. Culture, she tells us, matters more than many leaders expect. Different organizations often make decisions in entirely different ways, creating friction that financial models cannot predict. She also learned the cost of pushing too hard. Her team successfully completed aggressive integrations, but Kunze tells us she underestimated the human toll and would invest more heavily in staffing and support if given the opportunity again.
Today, those lessons continue to shape how she approaches leadership, growth, and change.

CFOTL: Tell us about LegitScript. What’s this company about?
Kunze: LegitScript is a really cool company. It’s mission-based, and our mission is to make the internet and the payments ecosystem safer. What does that mean? It means we’re looking for the bad actors—people who are selling, transacting, or producing illegal goods and services on the internet.
We focus primarily on high-risk areas such as online pharmacies, telemedicine, firearms, gambling, and adult-related businesses. We work with major platforms like Google, payment providers, banks, credit card companies, and individual businesses to identify bad actors and help remove them from the ecosystem, preventing them from processing payments or advertising online.
Read More
To make it more tangible, many people know someone who uses a med spa or takes a GLP-1 weight-loss medication. One of our business lines focuses on certifying those who sell medicine online and ensuring they are legitimate pharmacists, licensed physicians, or sourcing medications from certified pharmacies. Ultimately, it’s about protecting consumers and helping ensure they receive legitimate products and services.
CFOTL: Tell us a little about the company’s capital structure over time. Could you share some of that history?
Kunze: The company was founder-built and founder-owned. The founder eventually sold the business to private equity, and today we’re operating under our second private-equity ownership cycle.
CFOTL: If you had to boil it down, what’s driving growth inside the business today?
Kunze: There are a few drivers. First, AI is making it easier to be a bad actor. You can spin up a website and appear to be selling legitimate products in a matter of minutes. As a result, the need for organizations that can identify bad actors and help remove them from the ecosystem continues to grow.
Another major driver is the continued expansion of telemedicine and telehealth since COVID. A significant portion of healthcare interactions now occur virtually. That creates a need for stronger controls and certification processes to ensure providers are legitimate and consumers are receiving real healthcare services and authentic medications.
CFOTL: We always like to ask about metrics. What are the input metrics you watch most closely?
Kunze: There are several. As a SaaS business, we monitor the standard metrics such as gross retention, net retention, and overall growth. What’s particularly important for us is that we operate three distinct product lines, so I spend a great deal of time evaluating product-line performance.
Product-line reporting is much harder than many people realize. This is probably the fifth company where I’ve worked to build reporting that goes beyond contribution margin and all the way down to understanding what each product line contributes to the bottom line. Each of our product lines is at a different stage of its lifecycle. One is growing very quickly, one is relatively stable, and another is dealing with pricing pressure.
That creates important resource-allocation decisions. We don’t want to starve a fast-growing product line in order to support another area unnecessarily. A significant part of my focus is understanding those tradeoffs, evaluating performance at the product-line level, and making sure we’re investing resources where they’ll create the greatest long-term value.

LegitScript Certification Applications Rise 59%, Led by 101% Growth in Telemedicine

Certification demand rises as telehealth expands into new care areas and providers look to compliance to support growth.
September 22, 2026 9:00 AM Eastern Daylight Time
PORTLAND, Ore. — (BUSINESS WIRE) — LegitScript, the leader in merchant and product certification and monitoring in the advertising, e-commerce, and payment sectors, today announced continued momentum across its certification program as behavioral health, telehealth, and other areas of digital healthcare continue to grow and evolve.
Over the past year, LegitScript has seen a 59% increase in certification applications overall and a 101% increase in telemedicine applications specifically. The growth comes as telehealth has expanded into a much broader ecosystem of providers, infrastructure platforms, and specialty healthcare companies, creating new ways for businesses to reach patients and grow.
“We’re seeing companies think about certification earlier than they used to,” said Scott Roth, CEO of LegitScript. “When you’re building a business, you want to know from the start that you’ll be able to advertise, accept payments, and reach the people you serve. More companies are recognizing that compliance needs to be part of that foundation.”
That demand is translating into continued certification growth, with total certifications up 43% over the past year and telemedicine certifications up 80%. LegitScript also recently surpassed 10,000 certified websites across healthcare, addiction treatment, and other highly regulated industries.
Telehealth is also expanding the types of care that can be delivered virtually, with behavioral health offering one example of how care models are changing. LegitScript has seen that growth firsthand, with Addiction Treatment Certifications up 80%. Mental health providers are adding substance use disorder treatment services, substance use disorder treatment providers are expanding into broader behavioral health, and new models are emerging to address both. That is happening alongside significant growth in the broader behavioral health market, which is projected to grow from $185.03 billion in 2025 to $332.77 billion by 2034.
“As providers add services, launch new models, and enter new markets, they can also encounter different regulatory requirements, advertising policies, and payment considerations”, said Jaylene Kunze,  Chief Operating and Financial Officer of LegitScript. “Addressing those requirements earlier can help make compliance part of the growth process rather than something businesses must revisit later.”

COFO Era: Why a Risky, Rewarding Dual Role Is Taking Over the C-Suite
July 24, 2026
Author: Anthony Noto | Photos: Global Finance Media
Image 5: TwitterImage 6: FacebookImage 7: LinkedInImage 8: Email
Finance leaders are taking over operations—and the new COFO role isn't a simple shortcut.
There’s a new acronym roaming the C-suite. The so-called COFO — a hybrid chief operating and financial officer — is more common than ever, marking a structural shift in how companies are deciding who runs the business. But the combined role is a risky one: it works far better going one direction than the other, industry watchers tell _Global Finance_.
Salesforce made it official last year. The San Francisco-based company named Robin Washington its first COFO — tasking a 30-year finance veteran with steering both the balance sheet and the company’s artificial intelligence (AI) and digital-labor transformation.
PayPal, headquartered in San Jose, California, took a similar route. The company expanded CFO Jamie Miller’s mandate to cover operations as well as finance, putting one executive in charge of the strategic growth initiatives that used to require two separate memos and a joint meeting to sort out. Two very different companies, same conclusion: the boss who understands the cash is likely the person who’s expected to move it.
While some observers view this trend as temporary, many industry leaders see the hybrid COFO as a permanent shift in corporate leadership.
“I do think this is a trend that’s here to stay,” said Jaylene Kunze, COFO at Portland, Oregon-based LegitScript, a risk management service.
For decades, the CFO and COO occupied a kind of awkward office marriage: sharing a roof, splitting the chores, occasionally blaming each other when the numbers didn’t add up.
“Historically, the CFO and COO were often set up to work against each other by default since each one’s success depended on the other, but neither had the full picture needed to make the best decisions for the company,” Kunze added.
That being said: Does the COO job disappear? Kunze calls “operational acumen and a real connection” to the business as “essential.” However, she argues the CFO seat has evolved past spreadsheets and GAAP.
“That’s exactly why the COFO role is emerging as such a powerful one,” she said. “It’s not enough to build the model; you must know what growth targets you’re driving toward and which levers to pull, when, and how.”
‘A Whole New Job’
Executive coach Edith Hamilton, who works with CFOs and COOs at NEXT New Growth, noticed the same pattern.
“It’s not title inflation. It’s authority redistribution,” she said, pointing to AI-driven process change as a major accelerant. But the honeymoon, she warns, is short.
“The second emotion is, ‘Oh dear Lord, this is a whole new job.'” Boards, she added, flip the script overnight — from “protect the numbers” to “use your authority to change the business.”
Her verdict: durable, but not universal. “It will work in companies where finance and operations need to be welded together — not merely coordinated.”
Sierra Hinson has been living this arrangement for over a decade under various titles. Most recently, as a “fractional CFOO” through her firm, Additive Insights. Her reaction to the sudden buzz? “What took so long?” Splitting finance and operations creates blind spots and slows everyone down, she said. And it shows up at the worst possible moment — the exit. “In a transaction, buyers look for inconsistency between what the financials say and what the operations show,” she said. “The title is the easy part — the track record is not.”
Missing the Point
Not everyone’s convinced the direction of travel could reverse. Ariela Tannenbaum, former CFO at Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati and now a profitability architect, thinks the whole debate is arguing about the wrong things. “The COFO debate misses the point on two counts,” she said. “First, titles. Whether you call it inflation or evolution, a title reflects accountability, not capability. The higher the title, the greater the responsibility. Rebranding a role does not dilute it; it expands it.”
Her second point takes aim at the assumption that AI is what’s really behind all this. “Faster information is not faster judgment,” Tannenbaum said. “A CFO or COO in a COFO role will spend exactly as much time reviewing, analyzing, validating, and deciding as before. AI compresses the data cycle. The thinking, judgment, and responsibility cycle remains unchanged.”
What’s actually driving the trend, she argues, is something more old-fashioned: good managers building good benches. “Great financial leaders already mentor, elevate, and develop their teams to the point where the CFO can spread his or her wings to take on an expanded operational mandate,” she said. Given the chance herself, she wouldn’t blink: “I would run the operation with conviction through the financial lens, where clarity lives.”
The Risk of Reversing the COFO Role
But Tannenbaum, like Hamilton, sees the arrangement working in only one direction. “Can an experienced CFO absorb the COO role? Absolutely,” she said. “Capital discipline, resource allocation, performance accountability — these are financial constructs applied operationally.”
The reverse, however, is not symmetrical.
A COO assuming the COFO role introduces real risk: technical gaps in financial analysis, regulatory exposure, and the kind of judgment calls that only come from deep financial experience.
Her bottom line: “The COFO is not a shortcut. But it works in one direction far better than the other.” And for companies simply focused on saving a salary line rather than building real bench strength, she has a warning dressed up as a punchline: “Can’t find two great executives? Look under the light.”
Which brings the debate back to a question. Firms like Ridgeway Financial Service ask CEOs: does your team just report the numbers, or help run the business? Increasingly, in this new hybrid role, the answer is both — same office, same person, one very full inbox.

What Is Telehealth Infrastructure-as-a-Service (TIaaS) — and Does Your Platform Qualify for an Enterprise Referral Partnership?

There’s a category of company that sits at the center of the digital health economy that hasn’t always had a name for itself. These companies build the white-label technology that other healthcare brands run on, providing the clinical infrastructure, the prescription fulfillment network, the EHR integrations, and the patient engagement tools. Their clients go to market under their own brand, serve their own patients, and build their own reputation — all on the foundation these central platforms have built. 
The industry is starting to call these companies Telehealth Infrastructure-as-a-Service (TIaaS) providers. And if that description sounds like your business, this blog was written for you.
telehealth infrastructure as a service TLaaS
May 27, 2026 | by LegitScript Folks
Defining the TIaaS Category
Telehealth Infrastructure-as-a-Service (TIaaS) is not a narrowly defined business model — it’s a category that covers a range of companies whose common thread is that they power other healthcare brands rather than operate as a patient-facing brand themselves. TIaaS providers include:
 White-label telehealth platforms that enable digital health brands to launch under their own name.
 EHR and practice management systems built specifically for virtual and hybrid care models.
 Prescription fulfillment and pharmacy network operators that handle the medication side of a telehealth brand’s offering.
 Patient engagement and care coordination tools that manage the clinical relationship between provider and patient. And the operational or clinical infrastructure that takes a new healthcare brand from concept to first patient visit.
What TIaaS providers share is that their clients’ ability to advertise, process payments, and reach patients compliantly is directly tied to how the underlying platform is built and how credibly it can demonstrate that to the outside world.
Why TIaaS Providers Are Thinking About Compliance Differently
The digital health brands your platform brings to market face a compliance requirement most of them don’t anticipate when they launch. Major search engines and social media companies require healthcare and pharmacy advertisers to have a LegitScript Healthcare Merchant Certification before their campaigns can go live. Payments companies apply similar scrutiny to merchants operating in prescription-enabled categories, specifically MCC 5122 and MCC 5912. Without that certification, your clients’ ads get rejected, payment processing approval takes longer, and their ability to start generating revenue gets delayed.
This isn’t a problem your clients can solve by adjusting their creative or targeting. It’s a platform requirement. And right now, most of them are navigating it individually, on their own timeline, without any infrastructure you’ve put in place to help.
That’s the gap LegitScript Enterprise Referral Partnership is designed to close, and the opportunity it creates for TIaaS providers who want to turn compliance from a client headache into a platform feature.
Does Your TIaaS Platform Qualify for Enterprise Referral Partnership?
Enterprise Certification is built for organizations that need to manage compliance across a portfolio of clients. For TIaaS providers, that means embedding certification directly into client onboarding, standardizing it across your book of business, and offering it as part of the value your platform delivers.
As a practical gauge of fit: If your healthcare book of business includes 20 or more clients that prescribe, dispense, or facilitate access to prescription medications, particularly in a digital, remote, or card-not-present environments, Enterprise Certification is the right conversation to have. The conditions your clients serve don’t need to be identical. Behavioral health, men’s health, women’s health, dermatology, weight management, and primary care telehealth are all well-represented in the Enterprise Certification program.
The structure of your platform matters too. Whether you operate a true white-label B2B2C model, a shared infrastructure with branded client environments, or a hybrid where clients customize on top of your core technology, Enterprise Certification is designed to accommodate the complexity that comes with powering multiple healthcare brands at scale.
Turning Compliance Into a TIaaS Competitive Advantage
Here’s what makes LegitScript’s Enterprise Referral Partnership strategically valuable for TIaaS providers: Compliance doesn’t have to be something your clients manage around your platform. It can be something your platform delivers.
TIaaS providers that embed certification into their onboarding workflows can reduce client time-to-revenue by up to 40%1 compared to the self-service certification path. For a client counting weeks until their first ad campaign can go live or their first payment can process, that speed is both a meaningful part of your value proposition and a concrete differentiator from competitors who leave certification as the client’s problem to solve.
Beyond speed, Enterprise Certification gives your clients portfolio-wide compliance oversight, a dedicated account manager, and a certification that satisfies both card brand requirements and advertising platform prerequisites simultaneously. For TIaaS providers whose clients operate across multiple conditions or geographies, that breadth matters.
The TIaaS providers seeing the most value from Enterprise Certification are the ones who have stopped treating it as an add-on and started positioning it as a core part of what their platform delivers.
What LegitScript Healthcare Certification Covers for Your Clients
LegitScript’s Enterprise Certification program verifies clients across nine compliance standards: licensure and registration, prior history and disciplinary actions, affiliates and partners, privacy and HIPAA compliance, transparency and advertising accuracy, legal compliance, patient services disclosure, prescription validity, and compliant advertising practices.
For TIaaS providers, this means the healthcare brands running on your platform aren’t just technically capable of serving patients; they’re independently verified to do so compliantly. That’s a trust signal that matters to the ad platforms, payment companies, and the patients your clients need to work with from day one.
The Right Time for TIaaS Providers to Have This Conversation
If your platform is already onboarding digital health brands at scale, the compliance question is already part of your clients’ experience. LegitScript’s Enterprise Referral Partnership is a way to get ahead of it, build it into your process, and turn something your clients currently manage reactively into something your Telehealth Infrastructure-as-a-Service platform delivers proactively.

The GLP-1 telehealth market has expanded fast enough that certification has become a differentiator, and Meant is leaning on that directly. The platform launched this week with LegitScript certification, a credential governed by nine core compliance and patient-safety standards that also unlocks advertising access on Google, Meta, and other major platforms. For a new entrant competing against a crowded field of GLP-1 weight-care programs, that certification is less a quality badge than a commercial prerequisite, and Meant is building its early brand identity around it.
The clinical architecture is worth examining. Meant itself does not diagnose or prescribe. Prescribing authority sits entirely with OpenLoop Health, whose licensed providers cover all 50 states and hold the final call on whether a patient qualifies. That separation matters from a regulatory standpoint: it keeps Meant positioned as a technology and coaching layer rather than a medical practice, which carries different liability and licensing implications. Patients who do not qualify for a GLP-1, which includes tirzepatide (Zepbound) and semaglutide (Wegovy) among the approved options, still receive coaching and the supplement kit. Nothing in the program, the platform is careful to note, is automatic.
The bundled model deserves scrutiny. Pairing a prescription pathway with a proprietary supplement kit creates an obvious margin question: the kit is included in every plan, meaning patients pay for it regardless of clinical need. That design generates a recurring revenue stream tied to enrollment rather than outcomes. Whether the coaching component delivers measurable retention or adherence improvement is the actual clinical question here, and Meant has not published data on either. The supplement kit remains, at this stage, more of a product-bundling decision than an evidence-backed intervention.
What Meant represents structurally is a bet that compliance credentialing plus wraparound support, delivered cleanly through telehealth, can carve out a durable position in a market where providers and payers are increasingly scrutinizing which platforms maintain actual oversight versus which ones simply move prescriptions. The real test will be whether OpenLoop’s prescribing data, accumulated across Meant’s patient population, eventually surfaces outcomes that justify the coaching premium or quietly gets folded into a larger clinical network’s aggregate numbers.
